children: *Wholesale Marketplace Faire Expects IPO in Next 12 Months
*Faire on Track for $730M Annualized Revenue Run Rate in 3Q
*Faire Plans International Push, In-House Fulfillment to Continue Growth, CEO Says
Faire Won Over Main Street. Now it Wants to Woo Wall Street — Interview
By Kelly Cloonan
Faire upended a wholesale industry built on trade shows and sales reps, paving the way for mom-and-pop stores to order merchandise online.

The San Francisco company is now sizing up a new challenge: going public. The startup, which had a valuation of $5.2 billion last November, expects a stock-market debut in the next 12 months, Chief Financial Officer Jason Lee said in an interview.
An initial public offering would come alongside rapid growth as Faire pushes into new offerings and expands internationally.

The company is on pace for an annualized revenue run rate of more than $730 million in the third quarter, up 45% year over year, and expects to break even on earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization in the fourth quarter.

For much of the retail industry, e-commerce became a dominant force decades ago as shoppers jumped at the chance to order everything from groceries to clothing at the click of a button. That isn't the case for wholesale, the process by which retailers order goods to stock their own shelves.

"All of the innovation in retail has really been focused on the consumer," Faire's co-founder and Chief Executive Max Rhodes said in an interview. "No one had really been focused on how to connect brands to retailers."

In other words, the wholesale industry hasn't changed for more than a century, as Rhodes puts it. Local stores still largely source their inventory by traveling to trade shows and calling up sales representatives, and have little buying power compared with bigger, national chains that purchase products in bulk.
Faire was founded in 2017 to bring that cumbersome and time-intensive process online, Rhodes said.

Hundreds of thousands of retailers such as book stores, boutiques and grocery stores now order products from a swath of both emerging and established brands on the company's platform. That scale lets Faire negotiate lower prices and better payment terms to help its customers compete with larger players, Rhodes said.

But the key benefit of Faire's platform, according to Rhodes, is the wealth of data it has collected. The platform uses years of sell-through data from retailers to match them with products they like, and that will actually sell in their stores, he said.

"That combo requires a huge, huge amount of data," Rhodes said. "We have just gotten to the point over the course of the last couple of years where we have enough data and the technology has caught up to actually enable us to solve that two-step problem."

That data has been crucial for Faire's momentum, because retailers return to restock and order more of their inventory on the platform the more their sales grow. Faire makes the bulk of its revenue by charging a commission and payment-processing fee on orders, and says its platform is currently on pace to facilitate more than $4.5 billion in merchandise purchases annually.

The platform's lineup of products across decor, food, beauty, jewelry and apparel come from emerging brands as well as more household names, like luxury bedding company Boll & Branch and publisher Penguin Random House.

To keep up its growth ahead of an IPO, Faire is leaning further into its international footprint, which includes Canada, Europe, Australia and New Zealand, as well as new revenue streams. In 2024, company launched advertising--a business that now accounts for about 9% of its topline--to let brands promote their listings.

It also sees a particularly big opportunity to get into fulfillment, with plans to own a warehouse to store and ship out brands' products. Faire expects it could bring down customers' shipping costs by about 80% with the approach, roughly doubling their profit margins.
"We look for opportunities where we can use our scale and our data and our technology to help these retailers compete in ways that they've never been able to before," Rhodes said.
Long term, he sees Faire being the place where every retailer does the vast majority of their buying. In the process, he hopes it revitalizes main streets, including in his hometown.
"My vision is a decade from now, you walk down downtown Norman, Okla., and every storefront is open because Faire has made it so easy for these retailers to open up shops and to succeed," he said.
